questions.subject: Science
questions.stem:
Rohit has to balance a chemical equation for his practical record. He first lists the number of atoms of each element on the left-hand side and on the right-hand side of his unbalanced equation. His list shows iron: 1 on the left and 3 on the right; hydrogen: 2 on the left and 2 on the right; oxygen: 1 on the left and 4 on the right. Rohit tells his friend that he will first take up the compound in his equation that has the greatest number of atoms in it, whether it happens to be on the left or on the right, and then pick out the element with the greatest number of atoms inside that compound.

According to Rohit's list, how many atoms of iron stand on the right-hand side, and how many atoms of oxygen on the left-hand side? (ii) Which one element on his list has the same number of atoms on both sides? (iii) Rohit picks the compound with the greatest number of atoms and then the element with the greatest number of atoms inside it. Applying this to his list, name the element he balances first, and say how many atoms of that element he must end up with on each side.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) 3 iron atoms on the right; 1 oxygen atom on the left. (ii) Hydrogen, 2 on each side. (iii) Oxygen, which has the most atoms in the compound holding the most atoms. One oxygen atom stands on the left against four on the right, so he multiplies and leaves 4 oxygen atoms on each side.

questions.subject: Science
questions.stem:
Ananya was asked to make the oxygen atoms equal on the two sides of an unbalanced equation. She found one oxygen atom on the left-hand side and four on the right-hand side. Her first idea was to change the compound on the left, and her teacher stopped her: the formulae of the compounds and elements taking part in a reaction can never be altered. The only permitted move, her teacher said, is to place a number in front of a compound, and to equalise oxygen Ananya put the coefficient '4' in front of the compound on the left. Her equation was then only partly balanced, since the iron and the hydrogen atoms still did not match.

How many oxygen atoms did Ananya find on each side of the unbalanced equation? (ii) Why did her teacher stop her from changing the compound on the left? (iii) Ananya placed a number in front of the compound on the left instead. Give that number, and name the two elements her partly balanced equation still needed.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) One oxygen atom on the left and four on the right. (ii) Because the formulae of the compounds and elements involved in a reaction can never be altered. (iii) She put the coefficient 4, and the iron and the hydrogen atoms were still not balanced.

questions.subject: Science
questions.stem:
Dev had balanced the oxygen atoms and now looked at the hydrogen in his partly balanced equation. On the left-hand side there were 8 hydrogen atoms, sitting in the four molecules of the compound he had just multiplied; on the right-hand side there were only 2 hydrogen atoms. To equalise them he decided to make the number of molecules of hydrogen on the right as four. He wrote the equation out again with the coefficient 4 in front of the hydrogen, and read it once more. Iron, he saw, was the third element left, and now it was the only one still out of balance.

How many hydrogen atoms did Dev count on each side of the partly balanced equation? (ii) How many molecules of hydrogen did he write on the right-hand side? (iii) After balancing the hydrogen, Dev found that only one element was still out of balance. Name it, and say how he knew which element to take up next.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) 8 on the left and 2 on the right. (ii) Four. (iii) Iron: reading the equation again, Dev found that iron was the third element not balanced, so only iron was left to be taken up.

questions.subject: Science
questions.stem:
Meera's friend thought that an unbalanced equation must always be balanced from left to right, and he began with the element that happened to be written first. Meera told him the correct habit: while balancing, it is often convenient to start with the compound that contains the maximum number of atoms, and that compound may be a reactant or a product. Inside that compound one must then select the element which has the maximum number of atoms. She worked through his equation this way, wrote out each step, and called the equation she got at every stage a partly balanced equation. Only when iron was the single element left out of balance was her work finished.

What did Meera tell her friend to begin with while balancing an equation, and what two choices follow from that rule? (ii) Her friend began with the element that happened to be written first. Explain, using what Meera told him, why that habit can leave more work to be done.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) Start with the compound containing the maximum number of atoms; it may be a reactant or a product, and inside it choose the element with the maximum number of atoms. (ii) Beginning with the element written first can leave the element with the most atoms to the last, adding extra steps.
